```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "The 90-day paying-customer goal favors A's buying motion. A sells a $9–$29/mo self-serve subscription to developer and SaaS buyers. B sells to municipalities, and B's own brief describes their procurement as slow and bureaucratic (RFPs, insurance certificates, cooperative-purchasing vetting). That is a poor fit for closing a first sale within 90 days.",
    "A's channels are cheap and native to a solo operator: Indie Hackers, Product Hunt and developer SEO. B's main channel is conference booths. The only cost figure for them comes from a 2015 prospectus, and the state-league booths cited are already sold out. B's fallback channel, a free-audit lead magnet, is one that GovAccess and CASO Comply already run.",
    "A has sourced, specific pain about incumbent pricing: Statuspage's split public, private and audience billing running to $1,499+/mo, plus an r/SaaS thread questioning a $399/mo manual page. It also has a sourced proof that a single operator can make money in the category (Instatus at ~$10k MRR).",
    "A has no comparable legal exposure. B's Case Against flags liability for compliance claims that a solo, uninsured operator cannot easily absorb. The layer with real pricing power in B, legally defensible documentation, is the layer a one-person shop is least able to provide.",
    "Both markets are crowded. A's saturation, including OneUptime's free tier and StillOnline at $9/mo, mainly limits long-run growth. B's barriers (procurement, liability, enforcement uncertainty after one DOJ deadline extension) block the first sale itself."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "B's demand evidence is two quotes from a single local news article about one county (Cole County, MO). The stronger of the two (Landwehr) says the county's response to the mandate is to 'just remove information.' That points to a no-purchase workaround rather than willingness to pay. The $7,000 Continual Engine purchase comes from the same county, so B's purchase evidence also rests on one data point and does not show broad buyer demand across the ~17,000 small municipalities it targets.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate confidence. A's competitive position is genuinely weak. A new entrant is effectively competing against OneUptime's free tier, and Instatus's growth is described as slow. Neither brief offers evidence of a specific differentiator or a realistic first-customer conversion path. A wins mainly because B's structural barriers (procurement cycle, liability, thin single-county demand evidence) are especially bad for a 90-day solo target, not because A's evidence is strong."
}
```
